classification.difficultyReason: The taught secant and tangent methods are explicitly prompted. Students must position tangents, choose readable points and interpret their gradients. The hardest demand is extending the flattening trend to a derivative approaching zero and connecting that to thermal equilibrium; this is a routine conceptual link supported by the earlier decreasing-rate observation.

content.prompt:
A bottle of water was taken out of the fridge on a hot day.
Its temperature started at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and started rising.

spec.description: Temperature–time graph reconstructed with editable smooth Bézier segments through the source-labelled positions; no function equation is supplied. Retains fine unit grid, heavier five-unit grid, labelled ten-unit ticks, axes and curve arrowheads, A–D labels and the distinct red source annotation. The origin O label is omitted under the graph convention.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal range 0–80 minutes; vertical range 0–40 degrees Celsius. Curve passes approximately through (0,0), (20,20), (40,30), (60,35), (80,37.5), increasing at a decreasing rate.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent source graph and red annotation only; supplied blue answers are excluded.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the average rate of change of the temperature in the first 20 minutes?

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Is the temperature increasing at this rate the whole time?
Explain how you know by referring to the graph.

answer.short: No. The graph becomes less steep, so the rate of temperature increase decreases.
answer.worked: The graph is curved rather than straight, so its gradient is not constant. It becomes less steep as time increases. At a constant rate of $1^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{min}$, the temperature after 80 minutes would be $80^\circ\mathrm{C}$, whereas the graph shows less than $40^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

. Give your estimate to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Draw a tangent to the smooth temperature curve at the origin. A suitable tangent rises about $13.9^\circ\mathrm{C}$ over 10 minutes.
$$\begin{align*}f'(0)&\approx\frac{13.9-0}{10-0}\\&=1.39^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{min}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Estimate $f'(20)$ using a tangent. Give your estimate to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
Draw a tangent at $A$. For example, read approximately $(0,6)$ and $(40,34)$ on this tangent.
$$\begin{align*}f'(20)&\approx\frac{34-6}{40-0}\\&=0.7^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{min}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Estimate $f'(60)$ using a tangent. Give your estimate to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
Draw a tangent at $C$. For example, read approximately $(40,31)$ and $(80,39)$ on this tangent.
$$\begin{align*}f'(60)&\approx\frac{39-31}{80-40}\\&=0.2^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{min}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt:
What do you think will happen to the value of $f'(x)$ as $x\to\infty$?
Interpret your answer in relation to the context.

answer.short: $f'(x)\to0$. The temperature approaches room temperature, so its rate of increase approaches zero.
answer.worked: The curve becomes increasingly horizontal, so the gradient of its tangent approaches zero. The water warms towards room temperature and its temperature increases more slowly as it approaches that temperature.
